 CORE
July 14, 2025
Julie E. Adams, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List indications for wrist arthroscopy.
List commonly used portals for wrist arthroscopy.
Describe arthroscopic evaluation and management of common conditions.
Introduction
Arthroscopy may be helpful in evaluating the extent of known or greatly suspected pathology,
for example, in the confirmation of scapholunate ligament pathology and the extent of
arthrosis before making decisions about reconstructive surgery.
Wrist arthroscopy is most commonly performed for a defined treatment purpose and is
appropriate for the management of multiple conditions.

In scenarios of uncertainty with regard to the diagnosis (ie, low pretest odds) after patient
history, physical examination, and imaging studies, diagnostic wrist arthroscopy may result in
more uncertainty, in that, incidental findings may be observed and the risk of over-
management of findings that may not be contributing to symptoms is high.
Procedure
Indications
Conditions Managed via Wrist Arthroscopy
Pathology of the distal radioulnar ligaments and articular disk, often referred to collectively—
along with a few other structures—as the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)
The Palmer classification describes the pathology of these structures in terms of the time
from the inciting event (traumatic versus nontraumatic) and the location (Figure 1; Table 1)

Illustration shows the locations of complex tears according to the Palmer classification of
triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tears. 1A = central TFCC tear, 1B = peripheral TFCC
avulsion from ulnar styloid, 1C = tear of volar ulnocarpal ligaments, 1D = tear of radial
attachment of TFCC. (Reproduced from Wolf JM, Dukas A, Pensak M: Advances in wrist
arthroscopy. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[11]:725-734.)

Type 1 defects are traumatic.
Nonspecific management (monitoring, symptom alleviation) is appropriate unless instability
is present (the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) subluxates or dislocates during stressing of the
ulna or with forearm rotation).
By the time arthroscopy is considered, the reliability of distinguishing traumatic (type 1)
from nontraumatic (type 2) lesions may be questionable. Type 1C and type 1D lesions are
uncommon, and their management is a subject of debate. Débridement often is
recommended; however, the rationale for débridement of a traumatic rupture is unclear.
Central defects (type 1A) are avascular, with limited potential for healing. The only surgical
treatment considered is débridement. The ability to reliably diagnose traumatic lesions of
the articular disk and the role of surgical management are subjects of debate.
Avulsion of the origin of the distal radioulnar ligaments (type 1B) can be repaired via inside-
out, outside-in, or all-arthroscopic techniques. Given that these injuries are very common
(many occur in combination with distal radius fractures) and tend to do well with natural
healing, the role of surgical management is a subject of debate. The ability to discern
deeper avulsions (eg, those of the so-called ligamentum subcruentum) and the utility of
doing so also are subjects of debate.
Ulnocarpal impaction
Central TFCC degeneration is increasingly common with age but also may occur in
combination with ulnocarpal impaction (Palmer type 2).1,2
The diagnosis may be confirmed arthroscopically, with cartilage changes observed on the
proximal, ulnar aspect of the lunate.
Some studies include changes in the lunotriquetral ligament in the spectrum of ulnocarpal
impaction; however, this inclusion is a subject of debate. In this concept, load transmission
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
3/17

from the ulnar forearm to the ulnar aspect of the carpus can contribute to lunotriquetral
ligament disruption, which may translate to lesions of the cartilage at the capitohamate
interval. Although some MRI findings may be present and correlate with arthroscopic
visualization, it remains unclear if findings always correlate with symptoms, and some joints
have findings without symptoms.
The distal aspect of the ulna may be removed arthroscopically through the defect of a large
TFCC tear, using DRUJ portals, or via an open approach to reduce the potential for impaction
(wafer procedure). Alternative procedures performed to manage this condition include
diaphyseal or metaphyseal ulnar shortening osteotomy.
Distal radius fracture
Arthroscopic evaluation of distal radius fractures can aid in assessment of intra-articular
fracture alignment; however, comparative studies and evidence suggesting any improvement
in outcomes over imaging studies alone are limited.
Arthroscopy also allows the evaluation of concomitant intra-articular ligament injuries.
Changes in the scapholunate ligament, the lunotriquetral ligament, and the TFCC are
common incidental findings, and unimportant changes related to the injury also may exist.
Whether diagnosis and scapholunate-specific management improve symptoms or physiology
remains unclear. The radiocarpal and midcarpal joints are visualized for completeness if
intercarpal ligaments are to be fully assessed.
Scaphoid fractures and nonunions—Arthroscopic evaluation of the scaphoid waist via the
midcarpal portal allows for confirmation of fracture reduction at the time of fixation
(percutaneous). Visualization of the radiocarpal joint can confirm that the screw is not
prominent beyond the cartilage surface of the scaphoid. Techniques for arthroscopic
evaluation and management, including bone grafting of scaphoid nonunions, have been
described.
Chondral lesion/loose body
Loose bodies, which are rare in the wrist, may be removed arthroscopically. The surgeon
should be careful not to mistake a loose body, which may cause symptoms, with the fibrous
union of an avulsion fracture, such as a triquetral avulsion fracture or an ulnar styloid
nonunion, which is generally asymptomatic and not a source of pain or problems.
Wrist ganglion
Dorsal wrist ganglia may be managed arthroscopically, with visualization from the 6R (or 4-5)
portal, and débridement via the 3-4 portal, which typically coincides with the location of the
stalk of the lesion. The stalk is not always identified; however, arthroscopic excision of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
4/17

capsular tissue adjacent to the ganglion leads to satisfactory results, with a recurrence rate
comparable to that of open techniques.
Care is taken to avoid iatrogenic injury to the extensor tendons.
Volar wrist ganglia originate at the radiocarpal or scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal (STT) joints. The
ganglia originating at the radiocarpal joint, which are localized more proximally, may be
managed via arthroscopic débridement through the radioscaphocapitate and the long
radiolunate ligament interval.
Ligament injury
Diagnosis of scapholunate and lunotriquetral ligament pathology is complex. In the context
of wrist arthroscopy, this discussion is limited to noting that wrist arthroscopy is considered
the reference standard for diagnosis. Attention to the potential advantages and
disadvantages of diagnostic wrist arthroscopy is warranted.
The Geissler classification commonly is used to grade scapholunate and lunotriquetral
pathology during arthroscopy based on the appearance of the ligament intervals and the
ability to place or pass a probe or arthroscope through them (Table 2).

AP = anatomopathologic, DIC = dorsal intercarpal ligament, DISI = dorsal intercalated
segmental instability, DRC = dorsoradiocarpal, LRL = long radiolunate, MC = midcarpal, RC =
radiocarpal, RSC = radioscaphocapitate, SL = scapholunate, SLIOL = scapholunate
interosseous ligament, ST = scaphotrapezial, TH = triquetrohamate.
Ongoing discussion deliberates the interobserver reliability and the prognostic value of these
classifications systems, as well as the potential advantages and disadvantages of
management.
Radiocarpal arthrosis
Early scapholunate advanced collapse pattern arthritis at the radial styloid-scaphoid joint can
be managed via arthroscopic styloidectomy.
Occasionally, this procedure is combined with additional management of the scapholunate
advanced collapse or scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse wrist.
Arthroscopic proximal row carpectomy has been described.
Pisotriquetral arthrosis
Pisotriquetral arthrosis may be managed via pisiform excision.
Excision can be performed in an open fashion. Alternatively, the pisiform can be identified
and excised arthroscopically in some patients with sufficiently lax ligaments to allow the
arthroscope to reach the pisiform.
Synovectomy for inflammatory arthropathy
In the rare circumstance in which it is considered for rheumatoid arthritis or another
inflammatory arthropathy, arthroscopic synovectomy may allow for more thorough
synovectomy than open exposure because it affords improved visualization and access.
With the excellent medical treatment options available, synovectomy is limited to the very
uncommon circumstance of notable persistent synovitis, in the context of long-standing
optimal medical management.
Infection—Arthroscopic débridement and irrigation may be an effective treatment option for
patients with wrist joint infection. It may be particularly useful in patients in whom the
differential diagnosis is infection versus acute crystalline arthropathy.
Contraindications
Relative or potential contraindications include insufficient experience or skill in performing the
procedure, a condition that is better managed via an alternative approach, and insufficient
arthroscopic equipment.

Techniques
Patient Positioning and Preoperative Preparation
Positioning: supine, using a traction tower, with 10 lb of traction to the fingers
Equipment: 30° small-joint (2.4-mm to 2.9-mm) arthroscope
Fluid typically is infused through the arthroscope and may be infused through a pump or
gravity.
Some authors advocate dry wrist arthroscopy, which is particularly helpful if fluid
extravasation may be an issue. such as in patients with a distal radius fracture. This
technique may be particularly advantageous in patients in whom an open procedure may be
planned after arthroscopy or in patients with a fracture in whom fluid extravasation may be
particularly problematic.
Skin markings—The following key landmarks are marked after finger traction has been
applied: the Lister tubercle; the path of the extensor pollicis longus tendon; the extensor carpi
ulnaris; the radiocarpal joint at the scapholunate ligament interval, identified as a palpable soft
spot approximately 1 cm distal to the Lister tubercle; the radial midcarpal portal, identified as
a palpable soft spot 1 cm distal to the radiocarpal joint; and the ulnar midcarpal portal,
identified as a palpable soft spot at the same proximal distal level as the radial midcarpal
portal but in line with the fourth ray.
Portals
The portals are named for their relationship to the dorsal compartments (Figure 2)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
8/17

Figure 2
Illustration shows the standard wrist arthroscopy portals. (Reproduced from Goldfarb CA:
Wrist arthroscopy, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 393-396.)
Portals are created via incision of the skin only and hemostat dissection through the soft
tissues and the capsule. A blunt trocar then is placed into the joint.
For wrist arthroscopy, a radial radiocarpal portal (typically the 3-4 portal) and an ulnar
radiocarpal portal (either the 4-5 portal or the 6R portal) typically are used in combination with
two midcarpal portals (radial and ulnar midcarpal portals).
The 3-4 portal is located approximately 1 cm distal to the Lister tubercle. The superficial
branch of the radial nerve is approximately 16 mm (5 to 22 mm) from the 3-4 portal (Figures
3 and 4).

Figure 4
Arthroscopic image from the 3-4 portal, in the ulnar direction, shows assessment of
triangular fibrocartilage complex tension during the trampoline test. (Image copyright
Charles A. Goldfarb, MD, St. Louis, MO.)
The 4-5 portal is located between the fourth and fifth extensor compartments.
The 6R portal is located just radial to the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon. The dorsal sensory
branch of the ulnar nerve is approximately 8 mm (0 to 14 mm) from the 6R portal.
The following radiocarpal portals are used less commonly because they are associated with a
higher risk of neurovascular injury:
1-2 portal: potential risk of injury to the superficial branch of the radial nerve with potential
for radial artery injury
6U portal: high risk of injury to the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve if used as a
working portal; commonly used as an outflow portal via an 18-gauge needle
Radial and ulnar midcarpal portals—Approximately 1 to 1.5 cm distal to the 3-4 portal and
the 4-5 portal; useful for evaluating and visualizing the relationship between the scaphoid
and the lunate (scapholunate ligament) and the lunate and the triquetrum (lunotriquetral

9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
11/17

ligament) and the adequacy of scaphoid reduction in waist fractures (Figure 5). The ulnar
midcarpal joint may be easier to enter than the radial midcarpal portal.
Figure 5
Arthroscopic image from the radial midcarpal portal shows the position of the scapholunate
interval in the center, with the scaphoid only just visible on the right and the lunate on the
left. A small portion of the capitate is visualized above. (Image copyright Charles A. Goldfarb,
MD, St. Louis, MO.)
Other midcarpal portals used less commonly may include the volar midcarpal portal and the
STT portal, which is made in line with the radial aspect of the index metacarpal just ulnar to
the extensor pollicis longus tendon at the level of the STT joint. It may be used to resect the
distal pole of the scaphoid arthroscopically.
The following portals are used less commonly but may be useful for specific procedures or to
visualize specific structures.
DRUJ portals—DRUJ portals may be made proximal and distal to the TFCC, localized in line
with the 6R portal site. The distal portal site may be used to evaluate the ulnar head and
the undersurface of the TFCC, whereas the proximal portal, approximately 1 cm proximal

9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
12/17

to the distal portal, can be used to inspect the sigmoid notch and the articular neck of the
ulna.
Volar portals
Volar radial portal—This portal is located between the long radiolunate ligament and the
radioscaphocapitate ligament and provides visualization of the radiocarpal joint. It is
essentially directly volar and slightly distal to the 3-4 portal. To create this portal, an
incision is made longitudinally over the flexor carpi radialis tendon approximately 1 to 2
cm proximal to the wrist crease. The flexor carpi radialis sheath is opened, and the flexor
carpi radialis is retracted ulnarly to protect the median nerve. The portal is created most
easily by placing the arthroscope in the 3-4 portal and driving through the joint volarly
toward the interval between the radioscaphocapitate ligament and the long radiolunate
ligament. The arthroscope is withdrawn and replaced with a blunt Wissinger switching
stick through the trocar. The stick is then advanced into the volar incision to pass through
the skin incision as retractors are held to guide its passage. A trocar then can be placed
over the switching stick for placement of the arthroscope.
This portal is particularly useful for visualizing the dorsal capsular ligaments and
attachments.
May be particularly helpful for arthroscopic radial styloidectomy, in which the surgeon
can use the 3-4 portal and the volar radial carpal portal as visualization and working
portals.
Volar ulnar portal—This portal is adjacent to the radial insertion of the TFCC and enters
the joint between the ulnolunate ligament and the ulnotriquetral ligaments. The portal
placement is made via a longitudinal incision 1 cm proximal to the wrist crease just ulnar
to the digital flexors and radial to the flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar nerve and artery.
The digital flexors are retracted radially, the flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar nerve and
artery are retracted ulnarly, and dissection is performed to the radiocarpal space. A 22-
gauge needle is helpful in identifying the joint. The capsule is opened for placement of the
trocar. An alternative method involves visualizing through the 3-4 portal, creating a 6U
portal, and passing the trocar volarly through the ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral
ligaments.
This portal lies in close proximity to the median nerve, the ulnar nerve, and the ulnar
artery.
This portal is useful for visualizing the dorsal capsular ligaments and attachments and
the articular surface of the radius.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
13/17

During the course of wrist arthroscopy, visualization of the structures of the wrist should
proceed in an orderly fashion. Typically, this author visualizes initially through the 3-4
portal and uses the 6R portal as a working portal. Visualization and documentation of the
status of the radial extrinsic ligaments, the scaphoid and the scaphoid fossa of the radius,
the scapholunate ligament and proximal edge of the lunate, the lunate fossa, and the
TFCC and the ulnar extrinsic ligaments are performed initially via the 3-4 portal.
Subsequently, visualization through a 6R or 4-5 ulnar portal should be performed to look
back toward the scapholunate interval and the ulnar aspect of the lunate (for impaction
lesions) to document the status of the lunotriquetral interval and to provide good
visualization of the TFCC and the ulnar extrinsic ligaments. A shaver may be used to
remove debris or synovitis, and a small probe may be helpful in evaluating the status of
the ligaments and the TFCC. Subsequently, the midcarpal joint is entered. Typically, entry
into the ulnar midcarpal space is easier; therefore, this entry is preferred if the joint is
tight or difficult to enter. The radial and ulnar midcarpal portals are used to visualize the
midcarpal joint and to probe the interval between the scapholunate and lunotriquetral
ligaments. The surgeon may inspect the scaphoid and the capitate and often can enter
the STT joint. The lunate, capitate, hamate, triquetrum, and capitohamate interval are
inspected. The presence or absence of a separate facet for the hamate on the lunate
(type II lunate) and the presence or absence of chondral changes at the hamate, such as a
hamate arthrosis lunotriquetral ligament tear lesion, are noted.
It is particularly important to evaluate the wrist through the radiocarpal and midcarpal
joints if ligament instability is suspected because such evaluation enables a more
complete understanding and appreciation of the extent of instability. Most surgeons
consider complete wrist arthroscopy to include the use of four portals, namely, the radial
and ulnar midcarpal portals, the 3-4 radiocarpal portal, and an ulnar radiocarpal portal (4-
5 or 6R).
Hand Arthroscopy
Arthroscopy of the trapeziometacarpal joint is described as an option for evaluating and
managing fractures, ligament laxity, synovitis, or arthritis. The potential advantages and
disadvantages of arthroscopy are a matter of ongoing investigation and debate.
Arthroscopic-assisted trapeziometacarpal arthroplasty consists of resection of a portion of the
distal trapezium, with or without interposition of tendon or other substances.
Technique
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000026
14/17

The thumb is suspended in a traction tower, and the first dorsal extensor compartment, the
metacarpal, and the trapezium are marked.
Commonly used portals include the 1R and 1U portals, named for their relative positions in
relation to the first dorsal extensor compartment. The 1R portal is radial/volar to the
abductor pollicis longus, whereas the 1U portal is ulnar/dorsal to the extensor pollicis brevis.
After joint insufflation, an incision is made only in the skin over the portal sites, and blunt
dissection is made to the capsule. An egress of fluid confirms joint entry, and the trocar can
be placed. Most commonly, 2.7-mm arthroscopic equipment is used; however, smaller
instruments, such as 1.9-mm arthroscopic equipment, may be helpful.
Visualization through the 1R portal allows a view of the dorsoradial ligament, the posterior
oblique ligament, and the ulnar collateral ligament; whereas visualization through the 1U
portal reveals the anterior oblique ligament and the ulnar collateral ligament.
The superficial radial nerve and its branches and the radial artery are in close proximity to
the surgical field.
Arthroscopy of the other small joints in the hand is possible with the use of a 1.9-mm
arthroscope. The indications for such procedures are investigational and a subject of debate.
The metacarpophalangeal joint may be accessed via radial and ulnar portals centered on
either side of the extensor tendon, between the extensor tendon and the lateral bands.
Complications
Arthroscopy of the wrist typically is safe, with minor and transient complications.
Nerve injury—This complication is related to portal placement or suture of the TFCC. It
typically affects the dorsal sensory branch of the radial or ulnar nerve.
Infection—Uncommon
Tendinitis—May be related to portal placement or the suture knot after TFCC repair
Tendon injury—Improper portal placement may result in tendon injury.
Wrist stiffness—Uncommon complication of uncertain etiology
Mark as Complete
